utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We are to commence evidence of a new witness, and there are special orders in respect of this witness, are there not, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, there are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you ready to call the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour, and Mr. Weiner will be leading the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Can the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you be good enough to read the affirmation on the card that is being offered to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you would sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. We'll just pause while the blinds go up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to show this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Witness, is that your name on that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is that your date of birth on that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd like to offer that and asked that it be sealed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received and sealed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked P152, and it's under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we go into private session for about two minutes so I can elicit a few personal details from the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, during basic training, sir, what did you study?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I was an artilleryman working with Maljutkas. We were taught how to handle Maljutkas and different mines and also infantry training. That's the gist of my training.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any classroom training in Maljutkas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: For the most part it was in the classroom that I learned about Maljutkas, but not all the time. For about a month I was not in Zajecar, when I went to Kicevo to pass my "C" level training as a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's just stick with Maljutkas for a moment. Were you taught assembly or disassembly of the Maljutka system?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you understand it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Barely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about guidance? Did you -- were you trained in guidance or did you attempt to guide the missile yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, they did train us, but I didn't really understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a photograph and ask that you look at it. Witness B, could you tell us what is depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: That's a Maljutka rocket and also a device for guiding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is that a fair and accurate representation of what a Maljutka looks like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Basically, yes, but the Maljutka that we had was perhaps a bit shorter, something to that effect. Maybe its fins were shorter, but basically that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell the Court what does a Maljutka weigh, as best you can?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, they told us that it weighed approximately 15 kilometres [as interpreted]. They actually gave us the exact figure, but I don't remember it. So it's around 15 kilogrammes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what is the length of the Maljutka rocket?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: About this big, sort of. Perhaps this big. I don't know exactly in terms of centimetres or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the record reflect that the witness held his hands apart about 1.1, 1.2 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If it reflected that I think it would be inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We use a different measurement in the States. They tell me it's 75 centimetres

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we thought it might be .75 to .8 metres, so Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. we're -- that shows a Swedish eye as opposed to fisherman's eye that you must have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the approximate cost of a Maljutka? Did you receive any training on that or did they tell you what a Maljutka cost?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. They told us that it -- that this one rocket cost as much as a Lada Samara car at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: A Lada Samara, is that a Russian car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us the various parts in that photograph starting -- what is that base? It looks like a suitcase. What is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. It's sort of like a suitcase, and then this rocket is disassembled and put into it, and then this suitcase is carried around. At least that's what we did, one on the back, one on the abdomen, and in each hand one, and inside is the rocket. When the rocket is taken out, then part of the suitcase is dug into the ground, and it has something inside that is adjusted, and then the rocket is placed on that suitcase.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What are those two prongs in the front of that case-like object between the case and the rocket?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. It would be that kind of thing, like a prong. I don't know how to call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What does that prong do, prong or arm do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The rocket is stuck onto it. It is lifted and then it is adjusted in terms of the height that the rocket is supposed to reach.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Those flaps or wings on the back, are those on the rocket when it's in a case or do you install those?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: They are already on the rocket, but when the rocket is taken out of the suitcase, then these small wings or fins are opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is there any -- is there any wire on the device?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. When the rocket is fired, then a wire is left behind, and the wire goes from the device for guidance to the rocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What is that yellow object, pipe-like object, to the left of the rocket?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. It's like binoculars that you look through to see where the rocket is being guided.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, what is that object on the ground to the left if you're facing the rocket, to the left of the binocular-type object? What is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: That is the device or stick for guiding the missile, the rocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where does the operator stand or sit when the rocket is fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Near the guidance device.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And does he or she look into the guidance device and use the joystick to guide the missile or rocket?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, but there's a button, too, that has to be pressed in order for it to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you were not -- you had trouble or were not very good at operating the rocket. Could you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: In my battery in Zajecar, for the most part there were soldiers who had had a better education. There were only four or five of us who had completed only elementary school. For me, this was quite a bit of a problem. In the classroom, we worked on this kind of training about guidance, and we had to write a lot down in our notebooks, and I didn't really understand any of this. I only understood the very basic things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And last question, when you guide the rocket, do you guide it all the way into its target? Do you continue to watch -- I should say missile. When you guide that missile, do you guide it all the way into its target? Do you watch it the whole way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would like to offer this photograph at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is P153.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, since you were having some trouble with the Maljutka training, were you sent for some other type of training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. I was sent to Kicevo as a driver. Two of us from the battery went to Kicevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you complete the driver training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when did your basic training end?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: About the beginning of June, perhaps by the 10th of June, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you sent on any specific assignment in another area after you completed basic training? That's in June.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No. I continued doing my military service in Zajecar as the driver of my battery.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move a few months ahead to September 1991. Were you still at that same location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, until the 13th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you tell the Court what happened on the 13th of September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: On the 13th of September, in the morning, the alarms were sounded all over the barracks, and the entire army was lined up. We were ordered to hand over our weapons and to return some of our equipment. We had everyday working equipment and also the more ceremonial kind of equipment, to pick up just whatever was necessary, the basics, and that we would be sent for retraining, but no one could really tell us where we would sent to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you sent somewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. We set out on foot towards the train station in Zajecar - I'm not sure how many soldiers there were - accompanied by three officers from the barracks. We took a train to Titograd. We stayed there for one or two days, and then we arrived by bus in Titograd. We met a lot more soldiers who had come from other barracks, from Serbia, from Kosovo and so on, and then we were transferred in buses to Bileca. In Bileca, we were given lunch, if I may call it that, and later on in the afternoon, we arrived in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, from Trebinje, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: At the barracks in Trebinje, towards dusk all of us soldiers who arrived from Zajecar and the surroundings, they put us in several different batteries alongside with reservists who had arrived in the barracks on that same day, and there were only four of us Croats remaining in that battery. And I'm not sure how many other persons of other ethnicities, soldiers. Weapons were divvied out to everyone with the exception of us four Croats, and we set out towards Ivanica during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where is Ivanica located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I'm not sure in terms of kilometres how far it is from Trebinje, but it's about two kilometres as the crow flies in the direction of Brgat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In what state is it in? Is it in Croatia? Is it in Kosovo? Is it in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Ivanica is in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long were you in Ivanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: We stayed in Ivanica for about two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You say the word -- you used the word "about." Did you maintain any diary or record of where you were each day or what you did each day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: After you went to Ivanica, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: We left Ivanica and went to an rear area called Duzi. That's where we were stationed. We had guard duty there and nothing special in addition to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where did you go after those two months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand the question. Which two months?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were in Ivanica, you said, for about two months. Where did you go next? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Duzi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And after Duzi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: After Duzi, one day we received orders to go, and we reached Ivanica, the same place we had been stationed previously. We only stayed for a couple of hours, and we set out for Brgat, which was where we arrived at Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. What's the approximate date of your arrival at Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Mid-November, thereabouts. I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us what happened when you arrived in Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: My artillery battery left Brgat for Zarkovica with great caution. We walked behind trucks sometimes, and sometimes we had to crawl. We proceeded with great caution, however. When we reached Zarkovica that same afternoon, I was among the first to get there, and I noticed there were several soldiers, JNA soldiers, up there who were firing from automatic rifles. However, after a brief while, those soldiers disappeared from Zarkovica, and my entire artillery battery arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you set up any of the weaponry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, provisionally, for about half an hour, one hour. That's how long it took us to set up two Maljutkas and perhaps one or two recoilless cannons. That's as much as we could do given the time that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you do anything with that artillery and with those missiles after you set up the Maljutkas and the recoilless cannons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. Both the Maljutkas and the recoilless cannons were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Court what you mean by used in November?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Will you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Certainly. You said that you set up those weapons and that they were used. Could you please explain what you mean by the weapons being used.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. The weapons were used to target the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were there any officers present while these weapons were used targeting the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who was present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Captain Nesic, Captain Kovacevic, and some other lower-ranking officers. I can't remember their names, those who were with us in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anyone give an order in November to fire with those weapons on the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, I did, from the reservists. They said that Captain Kovacevic, Captain Kovacevic had given an order to fire, but I didn't hear this personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you say Captain Kovacevic, are you referring to Vladimir Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did your unit stay up on Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was additional weaponry brought to Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the Court's permission, could the witness be allowed to draw a diagram of the layout of the troops in Zarkovica, of the dormitories, the various weaponry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I've drawn what you asked me to draw roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could it be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you begin by explaining what that is, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: To the left from where I am you can see the Maljutkas dug in, in front of which you can see the operators. What you see in the middle of the anti-aircraft machine-guns, sort of, and to the right you can see the recoilless cannons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you point to the area where the Maljutkas were located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And then could you point to the area where the anti-aircraft gun was located.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you then point to where the recoilless cannons were located.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What are those box-like or rectangular figures? There are three of them on your drawing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: This here is one of the dormitories that we used to sleep in, and this is another dormitory, and here is where Captain Nesic slept, and that's where his command post at Zarkovica used to be. Something I didn't draw here was there was a cesspit here, and roughly speaking that's the layout of Zarkovica hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Were there any trucks on Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you show us where the trucks were located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The trucks were right here behind Zarkovica. Then here there was a road that the vehicle that brought us food took to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you use that pencil or if you could get a pen, and I'd like you to put a couple numbers on your diagram and then we can put it back. Could you please put a 1 in the area where the Maljutkas were located, the number 1.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you please place a 2 in the area where the anti-aircraft weapon was located.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you -- could you please place a 3 in the area where the recoilless cannons were located.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you please place a 4 on the dormitory.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was there an officers' dormitory there, or a communications area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. There was another dormitory there where the command was for Zarkovica, and that's where Captain Nesic was staying, as well as the communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you place a 5 on that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And finally, could you place a 6 in the area that's outside the mount of Zarkovica where the Old Town of Dubrovnik was, the direction? Could you please place a 6, or an arrow with a 6.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you put that back on the ELMO, please. Thank you. Okay. And just finally, could you just write "Witness B" and today's date on that piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Today's date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'd like to offer that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked P154.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Witness B, we'd like to show you another photograph. Witness, could you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: This is a photograph taken from Zarkovica with the Maljutkas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: That's at least what it looks like to me. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is the Old Town depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is that a fair and accurate representation of the way Zarkovica looked on December 6, 1991, in part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'd like to offer that photograph too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked as P155.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Witness B, how many soldiers were on Zarkovica or approximately how many soldiers were on Zarkovica with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: About 50. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what was the breakdown between reservists and conscripts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Will you please repeat the question? I'm afraid I didn't understand what you mean by "breakdown."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What were the percentages between reservists and conscripts of those 50 or so soldiers on Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The total number of soldiers there was about 50. About 60, 65 per cent of them reservists, and the remaining portion were conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, during those months in November and December that you were in Zarkovica and even January, how old were you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Had you ever been to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Had you ever heard of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When did you first hear about this place called the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The first I heard of it was when I was stationed at Ivanica, when the first shelling of Dubrovnik allegedly took place. That's at least what Captain Delic said, and he was the commander of my battalion at the time. He came over to see us once, my artillery battalion. He was quite angry, and he said that he had no idea why the Old Town had been shelled, if it had been ordered that it not be shelled. And that was the first I ever heard of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Captain Delic, that Ekrem Delic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't remember the first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was he the commander prior to Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that was the first time you'd ever heard of the Old Town. Prior to your military service, how many times had you been out of your municipality that you lived -- that you lived in? How many times had you been outside of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Perhaps twice, three times, three or four days each. As a child, sometimes we went on outings with my school class to the sea coast. That was about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When did you see the Old Town? When did you first see it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: When I got to Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how did it appear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: When I first laid eyes on it, it looked like the most beautiful thing I had ever seen in my life, and that applies not only to me but to all the soldiers present there. Everyone stood and looked in wonderment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, how is the Old Town or the Old City separated from the rest of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, it had walls, sort of. You could see that immediately from Zarkovica that there were walls, and you could tell the difference between what the new buildings were and the part that was inside of the town walls, encircled by the walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain on Zarkovica? If you began staying there in mid-November, how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: For about two and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the conditions were like for the soldiers in Zarkovica. Was there any set time to get up and go to work each morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No. We woke up whenever we liked, depending on the person, and in the evening you went to sleep whenever you wanted to, and the same thing applied during the day. Whoever was standing guard was just there on duty, and whoever wasn't was resting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, how did the reservists act? How did they behave on Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: They treated us soldiers who were conscripts in our regular military service quite rudely or brutally. I, as a Croat, received especially rude treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they do their daily work, the reservists? Did they do their tasks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: We conscripts who were not reservists had to do most of the work, clean the toilets, transporting weapons from one truck onto another, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did the reservists also do that work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Whenever they felt like it. When they didn't, they didn't. Then we had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was there much drinking of alcohol on Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How often was the drinking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The reservists drank every second or third day. In the evening they'd be drunk. Not only on Zarkovica but even before, at Ivanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about the officers? Did they complain or do anything about the drinking by the reservists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did the commander, Kovacevic, do anything about the drinking by the reservists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No. Whenever Kovacevic came to Zarkovica in the evening, they would all start panicking, saying, "Kovacevic is on his way." But they would just sing slightly more softly. It's not that they were behaving any differently. Kovacevic would just cast a glance their way and then leave. There was no special reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was there a lot of singing on Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What was sung?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The reservists were singing their Chetnik songs. They also sang folk songs. They had a cassette player with a large microphone that was aimed at Dubrovnik, and they played songs there, too, so they could be heard in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where were these reservists from that were drinking and singing and not doing their work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Only from Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was there ever any mention about Mijo Vucurevic from Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what about the reservists say about the mayor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Would you repeat the first thing you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did -- what did the reservists say about Mayor Vucurevic from Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: They said he was the mayor of Trebinje. I never saw him. However, he did come to visit the soldiers, even while we were at Ivanica. He probably didn't come to my battery. I did not see him. But a few reservists then went to these other batteries where he stopped by. They went there to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And after these reservists returned from their visits, did they say anything about the visit with the mayor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, whenever he arrived, they always talked about some kind of surrender and some kind of negotiations, that Dubrovnik would be surrendered, things to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's move on. Who was the commander of your unit on Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Do you mean my unit, my artillery battalion, or the battalion as such? I don't know about a particular unit. I know about the division, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the artillery battalion and my battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your particular battalion and the artillery battalion, who were the commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Captain Nesic was commander of the artillery battalion. He was commander of the division or artillery battalion. I can't remember who the commander of the battery was. It was a second lieutenant or lieutenant. He was a Bosniak; I can't remember his name. Whereas Radomir Kovacevic, "Rambo", was commander of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did the reservists say about Vladimir Kovacevic, nicknamed Rambo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: They said that he was very strict. I noticed the same thing. He was strict. He was brave. Things to that effect. Whenever he came, people would sort of panic. "Captain Kovacevic is coming." But he never shouted at them or did anything special, but they really were afraid of him, especially Captain Nesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you afraid of him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who was the deputy commander under Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Captain Zeljko Soldo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us move to December, December 5, 1991. Did you hear any rumours from the reservists on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Something like negotiations about the surrender of Dubrovnik. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, let's move to the 6th. Could you tell us what happened in the morning of the 6th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: In the early morning hours, I don't know the exact time, 7.00, 7.30, I can't say exactly, Kovacevic would arrive up there [as interpreted], issued an order. We were all lined up. If Dubrovnik would not surrender by 7.30, by a given hour, we would attack. We would attack the positions of the Croat forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, while you were lined up, was there ever any discussion from the commander Kovacevic that there was any fighting during the night? Was there ever any mention of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was there any mention of JNA suffering any losses during the early morning hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The reservists and the other soldiers, did any of them mention any fighting during the early morning hours or anyone -- any losses suffered during that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: During the early morning hours of December 6, from midnight on, were you awakened by the sound of any gunfire or shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: You mean during the night?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that? No, nothing woke me up. I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter' note: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated that on December 6th you got up and you were called into line. How do you know that that was on December 6th that this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, that stuck in my memory. It's a memorable day. It was St. Nicholas Day, according to our Catholic calendar, and a person cannot forget the 6th of December. I cannot remember that day for the rest of my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You said, "I cannot remember that day for the rest of my life." Do you mean you cannot forget that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, after you lined up and you were told that if there's no surrender that they would -- you would attack, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: We went to the positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did the Maljutka operators do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: They were stationed where the operators were, I mean the operators who were in charge of guidance, and they awaited further orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I was in one of the dormitories where there were some rockets and other weapons that were stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And -- and what were you doing with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: We were waiting until the attack began. When the attack began, then we would bring the rockets to the positions where they had been dug in. We brought them to the other operators who were preparing them for firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us about the beginning of the attack? What happens?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: First Srdj was attacked. For a while, Srdj was targeted. I don't know for how long exactly. Then artillery fire stopped at Srdj because the infantry set out towards Srdj. When the infantry set out towards Srdj, then automatically Dubrovnik was targeted from Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say Dubrovnik was targeted, what part or parts of Dubrovnik was targeted from Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: All parts. The Old Town, the New Town, and that island on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What type of artillery was used on the Old City? Please tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Mostly Maljutkas. Some recoilless guns, but then they redirected their fire to the new part of town on the right-hand side while the rockets targeted the old part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You mentioned cannons, recoilless cannons and Maljutkas. Was there any mortar fire in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. Mortars were stationed behind us, behind Zarkovica. They were firing too. You could hear it, but I don't know where they were firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, what were you doing while the artillery was firing on Dubrovnik, including the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Since I was an operator but I was not very good at that, I didn't really know how to do this, then I was just bringing these Maljutkas from the trucks that were stationed behind Zarkovica to that room where the rockets were, or I'd go all the way up to the positions and hand over the rockets to the other soldiers who would then put them in a position that was ready to be fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, within 30 minutes of the JNA opening fire on the Old Town of Dubrovnik and Srdj, was there any return fire?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I think that my learned friend is leading the witness by putting such a question. That is the first thing I wish to say. And secondly, if he wishes to base it on something the witness has said so far, that is not the case. This is a construction which has not appeared in what the witness said until now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The counsel, Mr. Petrovic, in my assessment, is merely directing the witness to a different and specific area by asking whether in that specific time there was return fire. So I cannot uphold your objection. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us what, if any, return fire there was towards Zarkovica that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: First tell us, when after the attack started was the return fire, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Five, ten minutes approximately when the attack on Srdj started.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, were you wearing a watch that morning? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, could you tell the Court about that return fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: When the attack on Srdj started, as I said, within five or ten minutes' time the Croatian side responded with fire against Zarkovica. However, not a single shell fell on Zarkovica itself. The largest number of shells was three or four, and they didn't even fall on Zarkovica itself but near Zarkovica, and that was all for all of that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness be shown the diagram P154 again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm conscious of the time, Mr. Weiner. Is this going to take more than a minute or so?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why don't we go ahead with the break and we can continue after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Because we will run out of tape time if we don't. So what we'll do now is have an adjournment for some 20 minutes, but first the witness needs to be allowed to leave the Chamber. We will now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness be shown the diagram P154, please. Could that be placed on the ELMO. Thanks. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Using the pointer -- using the pointer, could you please show us the area -- the areas where those three or four shells landed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: One of them landed in front of Zarkovica, one to the left, and one behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did any land within that military area on top of Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: You mean Zarkovica itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during the day, sir, during the rest of the day, did any other shells land on Zarkovica or in the area of Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when the shells landed, those three shells landed early after the attack started, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: At that time, I was in one of the dormitories.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was there anyone else in the dormitory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, there were some of us there. Quite a number of other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what were you doing there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: We took shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When did you realise that the other -- no more shells were landing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, it was clear, and you could hear that there were no more shells landing on Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So what did those people who were staying in the dormitory, what did they do when there was no more shelling into Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: We went down to where the truck was to fetch the rockets to take them back to their position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: With no shelling, were you able to move around Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, but with a lot of caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What were you being cautious about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Cautious of stray shells or stray bullets, those things mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were there any other -- were there any stray bullets or any sniper fire into Zarkovica during that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Not that I noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did any stray shells reach Zarkovica during that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, what were you doing during most of the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: As I said, I was in charge of bringing the rockets and the ammunition that was on the trucks and taking it to that room or to the positions where the rockets were stationed. Except when fire was returned by the Croatian side, those three or four shells, then most of us ran off and took shelter in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you place any of the missiles, the Maljutka missiles, on top of the platforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I brought the rocket to those other two or three operators who were there manning those rockets, and they had them mounted. I went back to fetch another one and stayed in the room until I received orders as to where I should go next. I did whatever I could to take shelter for the sake of my own safety until I received further orders to go and fetch more ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: During the day, did you ever watch or go up front and see what was happening from the -- as a result of the JNA shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you show us on that diagram where, from where you watched, the area where you watched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: This is where the first operator was, and that's where I went, roughly speaking. I was standing out about two metres from where the operator was, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you point to that again, please, that area again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies. So this is where the first operator was. I reached him, and I stood a metre or two away from him. I was standing next to him, but when he fired the rocket, I would stand back a metre or two from where he was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the record reflect that the witness has pointed to a line located between 1 and 2, the first line, a dot indicating a Maljutka closest to the number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many times during the day did you watch the firing from that position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Two or three times. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And for how long would you watch on each occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Sometimes five, sometimes ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you observe while watching from that location? What did you observe being hit or struck by the shells?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I saw that the shells were falling directly into the Old Town and on the ships and on the island of Lokrum and into the water in front of the ships. You could see that not only from my position at the time but, rather, also from the other position standing just outside the room. If there were people standing there next to that wall, it was perfectly possible for them to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you observe being struck by the Maljutka missiles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: What I remember most clearly is when one of the rockets fell straight through a window, if I may call it that, in the Old Town. We could see it from that far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say a window, was that a window in a building that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: It was a window on that Old Town, on the walls. That's what it looked like from the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you see any other rockets strike or any other missiles, Maljutka missiles, strike the walls of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What else do you recall? You've talked about walls, the windows or openings in the walls, vessels. What else do you recall being struck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Boats. Rockets were flying over the Old Town, depending on how good the operators were in terms of hitting their targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did any rockets or shells go into the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, while you were in that operating area, the Maljutka operation area, was there any talk about competitions among the operators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: You mean competition among the operators? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Please tell the Court what that -- what that discussion was about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The operators took turns firing the rockets. Anyone who wanted to was given an opportunity to try, even those soldiers who were manning the recoilless cannons could come up and have a go if they liked. Anyone was free to give it a shot. And they talked month themselves saying, "What shall we hit next?" And then one of them said, "I'll try to hit that one over there," and in case they were successful they would raise a hand by way of celebration, "I hit it."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What were some of the various targets, if you want to call them, that were part of this competition? What type of targets were part of this competition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: There were no targets as such. Anyone could target whatever they liked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were any boats shot at as part of the competition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, boats that were just outside the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about buildings? Were any buildings targeted as part of this competition or game?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't know which buildings you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, other than boats, what else do you recall being targeted as part of the competition? What did they try and hit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: That section of the Old Town, there were no targets. They were targeting whatever they could and whatever they felt like targeting. It was something like that. Some hotels were being targeted. They said the Argentina Hotel was on fire. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall any of the officers assigning any targets to the operators, any military targets? Official targets as opposed to the games and competition.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, no targets had been determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see a piece of paper in anyone's hand or a document indicating certain targets for the operators to fire upon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who determined or who selected the targets to fire those Maljutkas upon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Whoever was firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you saying the operators themselves selected the targets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did anyone ever mention that they were targeting a position in the Old Town that -- where there was a mortar or any positions where there were troops in the Old Town? Was there any discussion of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever observe any fire coming out of the Old Town, any gunfire, any artillery fire coming out of the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And we're referring to December 6th. Throughout the day, did you observe any artillery or gunfire coming out of the Old Town on December 6th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, while you were looking towards the Old Town, did you observe any flags flying over the buildings? Did you observe any flags?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. There were flags that could be seen even before that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know what those flags were or what they meant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Personally, I did not know what the flags meant, but the others were saying that those flags were there to protect the section of the town in the sense that that portion of the town was not to be targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was there any discussion among the reservists as to protection of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: On previous days, yes, before the 6th, and after the 6th also.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did they say? What was protected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The Old Town itself. I remember once we were stationed at Ivanica, it was after the 1st or 2nd of October when the attack on Brgat had commenced, and Captain Delic, who was the commander of the battalion, came over to our battery, and he was furious. He said, among other things, that he didn't know why the Old Town had been shelled allegedly with howitzers, given that the flags were there and that it was not supposed to be targeted. There had been an agreement not to target the Old Town and yet someone fired shells on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that was in October?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the 1st or 2nd of October. October.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you maintaining a diary in October as to what was happening, or any records as to what was happening on the various dates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can you give us an exact date when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, I can't give you the exact date, but I know that it was on the 1st or 2nd of October that Brgat had been attacked from Ivanica. Several days later, Delic came over to see us and that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did any of the officers on Zarkovica ever say that the Old Town could not be shelled or rockets or, I mean, missiles, Maljutka missiles could not be fired into the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But on December 6, rockets were in fact fired into the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you ever fire a Maljutka rocket on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did anyone ever ask you? You mention that all sorts of people were firing rockets. Did anyone ever ask you if you wanted to fire one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, I was offered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I remember Jovan Vukalovic was there, Djordje Gudelj. They were standing next to each other and they offered me to have a go if I liked to see what it was like to fire a missile, which I refused, saying that I was not a trained operator, that I knew nothing about that. They just laughed and I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Prior to declining their offer, did they ever tell you about any targets that you could fire at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No. They just offered me to try firing a missile, and it didn't matter what I hit, even if it fell into the water, it wouldn't have been an error on my part they said. It would just fly and hit something somewhere, that's what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they ask you if you'd completed the Maljutka guidance course or if you were properly trained in firing the missiles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, they didn't ask anything at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you that you couldn't fire upon the Old Town when they asked you if you wanted to fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, they didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you previously testified that some recoilless cannon operators also fired the Maljutkas on that day, on December 6th. Did anyone -- were you present for that, for the firing of those missiles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the first part of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You testified that the recoilless cannon operators also came over and fired some Maljutka rockets. Were you present or did you observe that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did anyone tell them what they could or could not target when these Maljutka -- I'm sorry, when these recoilless cannon operators were firing the rockets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, no one told them anything. No one warned them about what they could target and what they couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, we know that they were asked and you were asked. Who else was asked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: They offered it to anyone who was willing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did several people or did anyone who was untrained in Maljutka operation fire one of those missiles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where was Commander Kovacevic during the day of December 6th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: He was at Zarkovica for that whole day. He spent most of the time with the operator who was manning the Maljutka that was firing. He spent some of the time with the recoilless cannons, but after awhile, a brief while, he came back to the Maljutkas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did he speak to any of the Maljutka operators on that date? Did you observe that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. He was with then all the time talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How did he appear on December 6th? We're talking about Commander Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: He was furious. He was angry that whole day, all the time. He kept shouting. He kept running back and forth from the recoilless cannons back to the missiles, and he personally fired some missiles. He was very angry. He was always an irascible person, but he was particularly angry on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: For a correction on the record, page 36, line 18 says he was -- okay. They did correct it. I'm sorry, Your Honour. Now, sir, you said he fired some rockets. I'm sorry. Are you referring to Maljutka missiles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, about how many missiles or rockets did he fire on that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but certainly he fired ten at least. Certainly not less. Perhaps more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you hear him issue any orders on that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Please tell the Chamber what you heard -- what orders you heard him issue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I remember one particular order when he said on one particular occasion - I can't remember when the time was - he was talking to the operators, and he said, "Everything should be razed to the ground."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately what time he talked about razing everything to the ground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Perhaps in the morning at 10.00, 11.00. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did he give any orders in relation to the amount of fire that should be levelled upon the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: There was no limitation imposed. The main thing was to keep firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated there was no limitation that the main thing was to keep firing. Can you give us an idea of what he said, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: As I've already said, that everything should be razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you see Deputy Commander Zeljko Soldo on Zarkovica on December 6th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about Captain Nesic? Did you see him on December 6th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the time he was by the recoilless cannons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long did the firing from Zarkovica continue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The fire itself stopped sometime in the afternoon on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know the exact time that it ended or even approximate time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: If I say in the afternoon, that means around 3.00 approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, if you can, can you tell us approximately or about how many Maljutka missiles were fired from Zarkovica on that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Over 100. So it was 100 for sure, only more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, prior -- let's go back. Prior to the attack on December 6th, did the reservists say anything about Dubrovnik, specifically the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Before the 6th of December, they always said that this was a Serb town, that Serb churches were in that part of town, and that everything there was Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: After the attack ended on December 6th, was there any discussion about Dubrovnik by the reservists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. Not only on the 6th, after the 6th. Whenever there was any fighting in the Dubrovnik battlefield, whenever they would not manage to conquer anything, when they were sort of defeated, they would always say, "What do we need this for? It's a Croatian town. Let them have it," something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you observe any outgoing fire from the Old Town of Dubrovnik throughout the period of the JNA's attack on December 6th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, there was no fire. I didn't notice anything. This is what reservists -- reservists also said after the 6th of December for a few days, they were saying why did they shoot at the Old Town at all when not a single shell from there fired from Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak up or to get closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Witness B, if you could try and speak up a bit so the interpreters can hear you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, are you aware of anyone being decorated for their actions on Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I didn't notice anything except active soldiers who were doing their military service. They got a few days' leave, extra leave. Some got even 15 to 21 days by way of a reward. Only I and another Croat did not get any extra leave then, but I don't know whether that was for Zarkovica or for the whole thing, because we were on the front line, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How do you know other soldiers received leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: One day Captain Nesic lined us up, and he proposed that Jovan Vukalovic and others who were battery leaders and platoon leaders, that they should make lists of soldiers who should get how many days of leave by way of a reward. However, they all got this leave, except for the two of us who were Croats. Then we complained to Jovan Vukalovic who was commander of our platoon, because he was the only one we could talk to about some things and complain about some things. Of course, only on a one-on-one basis when nobody else could overhear. He then said that he would try to see whether anything else could be done, because allegedly the papers had already reached headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's take this one step at a time. When were you lined up and -- and people were advised of their reward time? Was this before or after December 6th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: After the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you complained to Mr. Vukalovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was it successful? Did you receive any reward after your complaint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, we did, my friend and I. I can't remember. Five or seven days of leave by way of a reward. However, we did not know about that until we were about to leave the JNA. I remembered another thing now. I think it was a reward for Zarkovica itself, because a gentleman, a soldier from Macedonia, Saso Janev, he was a squad leader, and he fired many rockets at Dubrovnik. He got the largest number of days, the longest reward time off. I think between 17 and 21 days. The rest got somewhat less.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You indicated that you didn't know about receiving a reward until it was time to leave. How did you learn that you were receiving a reward for your service in Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, since our military service had been extended by two months' time, we were supposed to leave on the 1st of February, 1992. However, since we got these five or seven days of leave, then we were to leave the JNA on the 22nd, 23rd, or 24th of January, and we asked Captain Nesic every day what would come out of that, and he kept saying he knew nothing about it until the very last day. That is when he told us that our reward leave had been granted and that we would be going home on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what day did you in fact leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I think it was the 22nd when we were supposed to go home. However, in the morning, we returned our weapons, and with Captain Nesic we came to Brgat on a truck. He went to headquarters, and he said, "Wait here." We sat on the truck all day, until late in the afternoon. He returned from headquarters and said that he was sorry but that they had some kind of celebration at headquarters and they had simply forgotten about us. Then we returned to Zarkovica, and it was only the next day that we reached the headquarters at Brgat yet again. Commander Kovacevic was not there, and then my release papers were signed by Soldo, my military booklet, too, and then we went to Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So your last day was on the 23rd, January 23rd, as opposed to February 1st?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The 23rd of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you said you were extended for two months. When were you originally supposed to be leaving the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I was supposed to leave the JNA on the 16th of December. However, since I did not go home at all, not for a single weekend or on regular leave, then I was supposed to get out on the 1st of December. However, since our military service was extended by two months, minus those seven days of reward leave, it turned out that it was the 23rd of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, after your papers were signed, did you have to see anyone else in the military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: At the barracks in Trebinje, we returned the rest of our equipment, our uniforms, whatever else we had, and it was not compulsory to go for vaccination. That's a kind of an injection. But we did go, my friend and I did, my friend who was leaving the army the same day. So we got this injection that people get when they leave the army and go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you return home, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. I think I got there on the 25th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, were you required to report to the local military headquarters or the local military office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately, within two, three, or four days, I reported at the office. I showed them my military papers, my military booklet, and then they wrote it down in their records when I arrived home, and then I went back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you have to report again some months later to that same office, without saying the location where -- where it is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, I had to in about three months' time to report at my office again in order to get a new military booklet, new military papers. That's when we got our booklet. As for this JNA booklet, we would throw that into the bin. However, when I got out of the office and when I looked at the new booklet, I saw that the date was wrong, the date of my return from the JNA. Those two months of military service, those extra months, were missing. I returned to the office, and they said something like that that's the kind of information they received from Trebinje by way of the date when I left. I tried to correct the situation several times, but no change actually took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I would like to show you this booklet, ask that you look at it, please, sir. Sir, is this a copy of your Croatian military booklet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And are the dates correct in relation to your service in Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: They're not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you've indicated you've attempted to correct -- have the dates corrected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. However, unsuccessfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to offer this, and may it be maintained under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This exhibit is P156 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Witness B, I'd like to show you this other document. This is your medical book issued by the Secretariat for National Defence. Sir, if you'd like at the second page of the Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian version, does that list the proper date what you received your injection from the doctor upon leaving military service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that would also be the second page in the English version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would like to tender this document too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That document is P157 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, have you ever testified in another court concerning the actions, the military actions, by the JNA which occurred on Zarkovica on the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where did you testify?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: At the court in Dubrovnik against the accused Zeljko Soldo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is that the same Zeljko Soldo who was the deputy commandant of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the outcome of that case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't understand what you said. Do you mean how this trial against him ended?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, the verdict, if you know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. 15 years in prison. However, not long ago I saw on Croatian television that he was pardoned a year later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, while you were in the military did you hold any rank or position while you served in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No. I was a mere private.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the 2nd Operational Group or 2nd Operations Group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar with a man by the name of General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar with Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you know the number of the battalion that you were assigned to back then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Was it while you were a member of the battalion or sometime after?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: While I was a member of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did anyone ever tell you what the objective was of the troops, the objective of the troops on Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did Commander Kovacevic or any of the officers ever explain to you why you were there and what their plans were to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Several times an officer would come, not of a high rank, of a low rank, and he'd sort of talk to the soldiers saying that the objective was to disarm the paramilitary Ustasha units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever learn of the objective of the troops on Zarkovica from the reservists? Did they ever tell you what the objective was in relation to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, after 1991 and 1992, did you ever serve in the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. I was mobilised in the action called Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: August 1995, approximately the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how long did you serve?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Four or five days approximately. I was at the front line. Then we returned to the barracks, and then I didn't feel well. I ended up in hospital. I was diagnosed with PTSP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Basically it's an illness of the nerves. I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to just go back and finish. On Zarkovica, back in 1991 and early 1992, how were you treated by the reservists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The reservists treated me very shabbily, both psychologically and physically. The reservists psychologically, whereas the other soldiers who were doing their service in the JNA who were ethnic Serbs, they also mistreated me physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How did they refer to you? Did you have a certain nickname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: They called me Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How often were you called Ustasha?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Everybody called me Ustasha, the soldiers and the reservists, except for the officers, of course. And Vukalovic, when he was alone with me, he would use my name when addressing me, but when he was with them, then they would always address me as Ustasha. They'd call out to me saying, "Ustasha." No other name for me existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You said you were also physically abused. Did any of them strike you, any soldiers or reservists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.
