Once when I was supposed to go on guard duty in front of the dormitory, a soldier called Cvetkovic - I can't remember his first name - came to wake me up half an hour early before I was supposed to take guard duty over, and I was already dressed and I asked him why he was waking me up too early, and then I sort of got up a bit, then he started beating me with a rifle butt, and I asked him why he was doing that. I said that I'd complain. And he said that I could complain to whoever I want and that nobody would believe me because I'm an Ustasha. Then I didn't complain, because perhaps I would have fared even worse. Even when I went home, when I did not go home that first day, had I returned to Zarkovica -- or, rather, when I returned to Zarkovica, then that soldier, Cvetkovic, and this other soldier, I think his name was Radivojevic, then they hit me on the mouth. And when I left by truck, they wanted to shoot after us as the truck was leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you returned back to your village, could you tell us how you were treated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. Back in the army they called me Ustasha, and over here some people called me a Chetnik saying that I had fired on Dubrovnik, that sort of thing. But those, in my opinion, were people who were perhaps even envious about something, but now the situation is much better in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What's the word that they called you back home? It didn't come out properly on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Chetnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: One moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Last question, sir. You were interviewed or you said you testified in the Soldo prosecution. Did anyone from the JNA ever interview you concerning the attack which occurred on December 6, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean. When about anyone from the JNA ever interviewing me?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did anyone from the JNA ever interview you concerning the firing of Maljutkas and cannons from Zarkovica on December 6, 1991? Did anyone from the JNA ever question you about what happened on that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Oh, right. You mean once I returned home from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, concerning the attack on the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. Back where I come from, I was interviewed by some police officers. I don't know who they were. And there were a couple of other interviews before the trial that took place in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did those interviews concern Soldo, the prosecution of Soldo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: When I talked to them for the first time, that was a month after I had returned from the army. The Yugoslav side still held Zarkovica, and I was questioned about all of that in terms of who was there and what they were doing. Once Zarkovica was liberated by the Croat forces, they only asked me about Soldo, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How, when you said you were questioned by police, were these Croatian police officers or Yugoslavian police officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Croatian. Private investigators, something like that, because they were not wearing uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the information you supplied resulted in the prosecution of Soldo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. The diagram which the witness drew, could that also be placed under seal? That's Exhibit 154.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the purpose of that being under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Since all of his other documents are under seal, I thought it would just be consistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Documents revealing personal details of the witness have one justification for being under seal, but that is merely a document concerned with the factual events of which he dealt in his evidence. I'm quite at a loss to see why it should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was just trying to keep some consistency, Your Honour, but that's fine. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You mean to keep the inconsistent consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's life in the UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think not, Mr. Weiner. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. May I have the lectern, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. B.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's how I'll keep referring to you during this cross-examination:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you get under way, may we just ensure or inquire, Mr. Petrovic, whether you would expect to finish by the end of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I regret to say I don't believe that is possible. However, according to plan, the way I have prepared this cross-examination and based on what the witness has said in this courtroom, I believe that I can complete tomorrow by the end of the first session. Perhaps even earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it would be important that you keep your eye and mind to time, Mr. Petrovic. The Chamber is becoming increasingly concerned at the length of time which is being spent on this trial, and in particular on cross-examination, and is concerned that a general tendency for the early parts in particular of cross-examination to be somewhat loosely structured and not really directed to essential parts of the case, and that cumulatively is having an effect upon the overall time of trial. As we've pointed out earlier, it's in your client's interests, as well as any other, that this trial not be drawn out unnecessarily. So with those words of reassurance, comfort, and stimulation in your ears, if you could concentrate on trying to deal with the essential points as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. I will do my best, certainly, but then I would also like to be told at one point when I should put an end to my cross-examination, bearing in mind your warning and your advice, which I hold in the highest possible esteem. What I wish to avoid is being suddenly interrupted, this making it impossible for my to conclude my cross-examination. That's what I want to say. I will abide by your instruction, but I would appreciate obtaining some sort of guarantee that I will be able to ask some of the key questions tomorrow, since a lot of time has already gone by today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think, Mr. Petrovic, that at any time in this trial there has been any sudden interruption of cross-examination. The rare times when there has been some firm hand taken is after long and careful warning. So you can be assured of that. We had rather thought that the nature of this evidence might be such that you could finish today. At the end of this second session. We may have a judgement as to whether our initial impressions are ones that we would hold to or whether you will carry on for a little time tomorrow morning. So perhaps you'd better get on with it now and use the time as quickly as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. B, first of all, I would like you to tell me the following. Who and where did you give your statements about the events that you testified to today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I gave my first statement at my local police station. The second statement also. The third was given before a court near to the place where I live. And the last one was given in Dubrovnik in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever testified during any trials in Dubrovnik before a Trial Chamber in the presence of an accused, a Defence team, a prosecutor? Is that how you testified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. The accused was also there when I testified. He was present in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just have the ELMO lowered a little, please, because I can't see the witness. Thank you for your help.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony today, you said that you were a member of the HDZ but not an active member. What precisely did you mean by that? How can you possibly be a member of a party without being an active member?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I never had my membership papers. I never attended any meetings, although I had been invited to a number of meetings, but I never went to a single one locally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How old were you when you became a member of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I had not even turned 18. I had not even come of age. So that's probably one of the reasons why I was not given any proper membership papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, why did you decide to join the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Because it was a democratic party in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the objectives, what the platform of that party was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Briefly, in one sentence, what were the objectives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: A democratic Croatia and the downfall of communism.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what VES means, military specialisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I think it's something to do with the battery, VES. I'm not sure, but it does ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would it be of any assistance to you if I told you that this was a military occupational speciality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. Now I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So what was your VES, military occupational speciality? What were you trained for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I was an operator and a truck driver. That was an additional speciality that I had. But my basic speciality was as a Maljutka operator.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you distinguish between the basic VES and the additional VES. You can even distinguish between the different kinds, can't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. After all, it's in my military papers, in my military booklet. It's right there for you to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Back in Zajecar, were you trained to become an operator by VES?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: That's what they wrote down in my military booklet, although that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you take any exams? Did you perhaps take any tests?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is that what they wrote down in your booklet in Zajecar, that you were a trained operator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How come you stayed in Zajecar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I stayed because I was a driver. My presence there was required. The battery needed me. There were about ten squad leaders left and ten privates, those of us remaining and the squad leaders said that new recruits would be coming. I drove the truck for the battery, and I was the truck driver for the whole barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which unit that was where you were in Zajecar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I appreciate you are eagerly getting on. There does need to be a pause, not a lengthy one, but a clear pause between the answer and your question and between the end of your question and the commencement of the answer because of the voice distortion protection measure equipment. So if you could just take a short breath.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, if you know, which unit did you belong to in Zajecar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which type of unit it was generally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: My artillery battery contained a -- our artillery battalion contained a Maljutka battery, a battery of self-propelled guns, and there was another battery, some sort of command, something along those lines; I don't remember. So there were those three batteries within that artillery battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What is the distance between Zajecar and Titograd? How long does it take to get from one place to the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Depends on your mode of travel. Do you mean by rail?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question is how you travelled.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: By rail. I don't remember exactly how long it took. I think it took more than a day. The train was very slow, too, and then people boarded the train along the way there. There were other stations, and soldiers kept getting on the train.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in your barracks in Zajecar in May 1991, a new group of soldiers arrived --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Will you please just repeat the month for me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: May or June?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: That wasn't my artillery battalion. My artillery battalion got new people towards the end of June. We had reinforcements, new people every six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Those soldiers, were they also sent to Titograd along with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Those soldiers or, rather, had those soldiers received the proper training at all to operate the Maljutkas and the other weapons that unit in Zajecar had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: They'd gone through some training, but they had not completed it by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So they'd not completed their training and yet they were sent from Zajecar to Podgorica together with you. Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What happened to the officers from your unit in Zajecar? Did they also travel with you, and were they also assigned to the same units which you belonged to later on? That was the unit that you devoted most of your testimony to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No. All the soldiers remained in the barracks in Zajecar. It was only three officers from that barracks that accompanied us as far as Trebinje, and when they saw to it that we arrived safely in the barracks in Trebinje, they went back. I know only one of their names, Jaldalski -- or Medarski.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So none of your superior officers since December 1991 to December 1991 [as interpreted] stayed with you. You were assigned to entirely new units, weren't you? How long did you travel from Zajecar through Trebinje to Bileca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I've answered that question already. It took us about two days to reach Titograd, up to two days. We spent one or two nights there, and we set out for Bileca where we only stayed for a short while. We had lunch there and then continued on towards Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that two of the soldiers from your unit fled en route between Trebinje and Ivanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who were those soldiers and why did they flee?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Those were my best friends in the army. Ante Situm from Imotski and Franjo Bolin from Djordjevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So they fled the unit and the unit was moving from Trebinje to Ivanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. We had already arrived at Ivanica. That was the first day following our arrival, and we were beginning to dig in and to work on the bunkers, but not too many people really working seriously because no one actually expect add attack to take place. They said we were merely there to watch the border. There was an agreement between those two, myself, and a fourth soldier, Prelcic that we would try to leave the JNA and that we would try to run away as soon as an opportunity presented itself. That was what we had agreed upon. However, the two of them went to a shop in Ivanica, the two of us, myself and Prelcic stayed back so they seized their opportunity to go to Brgat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. B, can you please just stick to answering my questions. My question was about them fleeing the unit while the unit was moving from Trebinje to Ivanica, wasn't it? I did not exactly require any further explanation. Thank you. When did those combat operations in the area commence? Is it true that on the first day of these combat operations 12 members of the JNA were killed in the very same place where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how those people were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Those people, that's at least what the reservists and lower-ranking officers said, this was back at Ivanica because the recoilless guns had been positioned too close to one another, so when a shell fell from the Croatian side on Brgat, that's when the soldiers were killed. And there were some people wounded too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that many shells landed on your unit on that occasion, shells fired by the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The Maljutka battery that I belonged to, seven shells, at least the way I counted them, landed behind us at Ivanica, some metres behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was that all, all the shells that landed on you that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about my own battery. I don't know about the other batteries.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear how many shells had landed on other units nearby?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that there were very many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you're referring to, very many, how many exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to help you with this now. Did you give a statement to the investigators of the Tribunal in 2002?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll read out to you what you said in that statement on page 4 of the B/C/S version: "The Croatian defenders at Brgat fired back by recoilless guns of the JNA that were in the higher positions. During that first attack, between 10 and 12 JNA soldiers were killed. Near our Maljutka battery there were seven shells that landed and missed us by about ten metres. After that we retreated and I stopped counting the incoming shells." You stopped counting the shells because there were so many shells that you couldn't even count them in, could you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. I withdrew or, rather, we withdrew, and there was no way for me to tell how many shells landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you retreat back to your starting positions because the resistance put up by the Croatian forces was that fierce?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Am I allowed to explain exactly where we withdrew to or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just please try to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: We withdrew allegedly because there were people who were dead there, and the Maljutka missiles that were firing at Brgat were rather unsuccessful, allegedly because they were moist and they didn't want to explode more than half of them. That's what people said. And that is why we were compelled to withdraw from Ivanica to Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why are you telling us today that you returned to Trebinje when in your statement there is no mention of that, none whatsoever? In your statement, on page 5 it says that you retreated and went back to the village of Ivanica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No. We withdrew from Ivanica towards Trebinje, and we stayed there, I don't know, a day or two and then returned to Ivanica yet again, because allegedly the officers said that Croatian forces had come to Ivanica. However, since this is a different border, then they went back to Brgat. When the Yugoslav side saw that, then we went back to Ivanica, to our positions there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, you rose?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just to correct -- apparent correction of the record. On page -- on line 17 on page 58, they said that the JNA were in the higher positions, and the word should be lower position in the English. It may make -- it may make a difference in the future. I just want to check on what the B/C/S states. The line is: "The Croatian defenders at Brgat retaliated by firing at JNA recoilless cannons that were at a lower position." And in the transcript here it says, "higher position." What does the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the B/C/S it also says lower positions. If I did not read it out that way, then the mistake is mine. It's unintentional, but that's what it says in the B/C/S too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Petrovic, as we have disturbed you, we might notice the clock and have the break at this point. How do you see your progress so far in your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's very hard for me to assess that so soon. There has been some progress, but it's very fleeting, if I can put it that way. There hasn't been enough time for me to give a proper assessment, but I'll try to focus on the very essence now, and then we will be able to tell perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would need a ten-minute break or so, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will hold our judgement then, Mr. Petrovic, for a little longer. Thank you. We will have break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We need to enable the witness -- can that be done after we leave? Yes. We will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness please be given P156. In view of the nature of the exhibit concerned, could we please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. B, why did you tell us --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. B, since I am being cautioned about this, too, when I put a question to you, could you please pause for a few seconds so that I could turn off my microphone before you start giving your answer so that we could protect your identity as you had wished and as is appropriate before this Court.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just before the break, why did you tell the Honourable Trial Chamber that you were in Dubrovnik at the trial that was held, Soldo's trial, when you were not there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I was at Soldo's trial in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When were you at this trial exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I think it was in the month of March 1993. I'm not sure, but thereabouts. It was in the spring of 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I will tell you now that I have the judgement of that court in front of me now, the trial of Zeljko Soldo, and this is what the judgement said on page 11. This is ERN number 00228896 in Croatian. This is a list of exhibits that was tendered during that trial. Sir, here we have a list of the witnesses that the court heard, and the reference is to four witnesses that were heard before the court during the proceedings, and then it says: "An agreement was reached between the parties to read out a statement that the Witness B had given." That is your name, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, and it is still my submission that I was there at Zeljko Soldo's trial in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I may be of assistance. If this is clearly stated in the judgement, that means that your statement, the statement that you had given elsewhere, was simply read out, the statement that you had given to another body, to another court, an investigating judge, or by request in a different way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I will proceed. Further in the judgement the substance of your evidence is examined and the book of rules is quoted in relation to examination of witnesses, dated the 1st of December, 1992, in front of the district court in Bjelovar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Will you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the statement of reasons attached to a judgement, the substance of your evidence is examined, and the pages given are 104, 105. That's how they were marked in Dubrovnik, the transcript, and this is in relation to the hearing of Witness B, compiled on the 1st of December, 1992, in front of the district court in Bjelovar. This is in the possession of the OTP, ERN 00229046.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately before I went to the court in Dubrovnik, I had given a statement in front of the Bjelovar court, but after that I also gave testimony before the Dubrovnik court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you misunderstand me. Perhaps you pretend to misunderstand me. Here we have a statement of reasons attached to a judgement, and the submission is that a statement was read out. My learned friends and colleagues and the Honourable Trial Chamber can have evidence to this effect from just about any lawyer from the former Yugoslavia. What this means is that a written document was read out, doesn't it? It means that the witness was not physically present before the court, did not testify viva voce.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I completely fail to understand this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on, then. How many times and to whom exactly in the police and before the courts did you give statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. Twice, I believe, in Krizevci, once in Bjelovar, and once again at home where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in Krizevci, which case did you testify in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, the case where I was during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In Krizevci, were you questioned in the case of the accused Zeljko Soldo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Not the first time, but the second time, yes, they questioned me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you perhaps prosecuted on account of your participation in the events that you recounted today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you were questioned, you gave testimony in the Zeljko Soldo case, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Each time you were questioned, it was in relation to the Zeljko Soldo case, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, with the exception of the very first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So what was the first time in relation to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The first time I gave a statement was in relation to the general situation as to who the commander had been at Zarkovica and what the Superior Command was, because the JNA was still holding those positions at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your memory in relation to those events, was it particularly fresh immediately following the period when all these things happened in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the statement you gave the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia in Bjelovar on the 21st of April, 1992, you stated that you had arrived in Zarkovica at the beginning of December.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Is that November?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That you reached Zarkovica at the beginning of December.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, not the beginning of December. It was mid-November.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to tell us why, then, you told the police that you had arrived at the beginning of December. You stated that clearly in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't remember that, that I ever said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you cautioned that you should read the statement before you signed it in order to be able to certify that the statement faithfully reflects your words and what you said the truth was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How come, then, the statement reads that you arrived in Zarkovica in December?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that statement state explicitly who fired the missiles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't have the statement in front of me. I can't tell you whether it's there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the names of those persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Those firing the missiles, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you enumerate the names of these persons and how many missiles each of them fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Jovan Vukalovic, Djordje Gudelj, Vladimir Kovacevic, Saso Janev, Cvetkovic. I can't remember any other names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And how many missiles each?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I can't say with precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: May I be allowed to remind you then? On the 21st of April, 1992, you said that Vukalovic had fired six --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is he going to refresh his recollection? If he's going to do that he should give him the document and let him read it and see if that refreshes his recollection. It's not an issue of prior inconsistent statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That would be the normal procedure, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I show him the statement, I have nothing left to ask in relation to that statement. Then what happens is he reads the statement, and what I want to do is see whether he remembers and the authenticity of what he said. If I show him the statement, then there's no need for me to ask any further questions in relation to the statement. I might as well move on then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can certainly ask him whether he recalls certain matters that you know are recorded in that statement, and if he doesn't recall them, what you do after that, then, if you are wanting to put to him what is in the statement is that you need to show him the statement. So you can -- has that given you enough help?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on the 21st of April, 1992, you said, as follows, that the total of the missiles fired was 26 from Zarkovica on the 6th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why then --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where does it say that in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Weiner, it's on 00229069, and there is a list of who fired those missiles and how many missiles each of those persons. So if you add them up, it amounts to 26 missiles exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It doesn't -- that doesn't say that it's listing every single person who has fired rockets or missiles. And he never said today every single person who fired missiles. That's taking it out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Name by name there is a list of persons who fired the missiles, and he referred to all these persons today. There are no new names on this list. If there are, please point them out to me. If there is a single name that has not been referenced in court today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: With regard to the list who fired, I don't see Vladimir Kovacevic here, which all his other statements talk about Kovacevic firing, and it does not say that this is the total list of persons who fired, and today he didn't say the only persons that fired were those that were named. He said the ones that -- they were operators from recoilless cannons that were firing. I don't see anyone here listed as a recoilless cannon operator.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be of assistance, I think the best way for me to proceed is to just move on with my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At Zarkovica on the 6th of December, did you see any other JNA officers in relation -- except for the ones you've enumerated today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: As I said, in the presence of Kovacevic I saw one or two other officers, but I can't remember their names, and I can't remember anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember their ranks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: You mean ranks?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I mean were they high-ranking officers, junior officers and specific ranks, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Those were junior officers, but I can't remember the ranks specifically. Whether they were reservists or officers, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So they may as well have been reservists; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. I'd never seen them before and I never saw them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'll read out what you stated to the OTP on the 15th of June, 2002. This is page 8 of the B/C/S version. "Also, I saw a number of other high-ranking JNA officers whose names I don't know visiting Zarkovica on the 6th of December."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That was in the afternoon when the shelling of Dubrovnik had already stopped. I apologise. I thought your question was in relation to the moment that Dubrovnik was being targeted. That's when I saw the junior officers. And later on in the afternoon, once the shelling had stopped, some higher-ranking officers arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On page 75, line 19 of the transcript, my question to you was: Which other JNA officers did you see on that day? If my question is unclear to you, then please say it right away. What did those high-ranking officers wear, the ones you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I saw them at a distance. I wasn't physically there, not a single time when the high-ranking officers arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were any of those officers wearing naval uniform or were they all wearing olive drab?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: As I said, I saw them from a distance, and I can't remember any specifics as to what exactly they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You were looking from afar. How could you tell that those were high-ranking officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Because that's what the reservists said, that some high-ranking officers would be coming to Zarkovica and that all of us Croats should go back to our rooms. Not that we needed telling on that day, because we'd usually be given advance notice when high-ranking officers were about to arrive, so we were never there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about never. I'm asking specifically in relation to the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So some reservists told you that high-ranking officers would be arriving, and you did what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I went back to the dormitory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How long did you remain there for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: This whole time, until they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did you know when they left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, the reservists said. They said, "Okay. Now they're gone." Or the other soldiers who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So it is your submission those high-ranking officers arrived in the afternoon, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you wear a watch on that day, or perhaps you were keeping a journal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, neither.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So how come you know they arrived in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the sun, the position of the sun, you can tell. Everyone knows what the position of the sun is in the afternoon and in the morning. If you look at the sun, it's easy to tell the time. It's easy to distinguish between the morning and the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you remember the exact position of the sun at the moment those officers arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, not this very moment. I don't remember the position of the sun then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But my question is: How do you know they arrived in the afternoon, and you say the position of the sun, and then my question to you is, do you then remember the exact position of the sun on the 6th of December, the moment the officers arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: This very moment, I do not remember the position of the sun.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you don't actually remember that they came in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Oh, but yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who among those high-ranking officers did you know or who had you heard of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Almost no one. I'd heard from the reservists about a man called Zec, but I never saw anyone, none of the high-ranking officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If you never saw any of those high-ranking officers, why then did you state to the investigators on the 15th of June, 2002, as follows, it's the same page that I quoted awhile ago: "I also saw a number of other high-ranking JNA officers whose names I don't know visiting Zarkovica on the 6th of December. I think they came in the afternoon when the operation almost over. I think I saw Milan Zec once or twice during the whole operation."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, that's perfectly clear if you read my answer again. I saw the Campagnola arriving, the vehicle, and everyone was saying that higher-ranking officers were coming and I should go away. As far as Zec is concerned, I'm not sure about his rank. I said I believed I saw someone who looked just like him, but I never actually said that I saw him in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, if there is a person who looks just like Zec, then you must know what Zec looks like or who he is, Milan Zec?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, I don't really know. I just saw him on TV about two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So two years ago, you were just watching TV, and you saw someone and then it dawned on you that you had seen that someone on Zarkovica on the 6th of December; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, something like that, from a distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Which means that 11 years later, you see a person on TV, and this person just happens to look very much like someone you had seen from a distance on the 6th of December at Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about this person, Milan Zec?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was there a time when you knew something about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Croatia four months after the events we are discussing, the transcript is dated the 21st of April, 1992, and the page number is 2209068 [as interpreted]. You said as follow: "Kovacevic was probably ordered to attack Dubrovnik by a certain general named Zec."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, that's what the reservists said. They talked among themselves, and they mentioned Zec, like I said. But I didn't hear this or see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So when I ask you a question, when I ask you whether there was ever a time that you knew something about this person, and I asked you precisely that two minutes ago, and you said no --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object. According to his statement, he is speculating, or he's repeating the speculation of reservists. That's not his memory of his personal knowledge of Zec, and he's maintained he doesn't know anything about Zec. In fact, he refers to him as a general, which he isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did the reservists say? What happened to this General Zec?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is what you've said: "Kovacevic was probably ordered to attack Dubrovnik by a certain General Zec, who was allegedly replaced later because he did not have orders from Belgrade for the attack."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Who did they replace?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Zec, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Possibly. At this moment, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, did the reservists tell you that Zec had ordered the attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When -- when did the reservists tell you that Zec ordered the attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Probably later. I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did they tell you, how much later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did the reservists actually tell you anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: You mean about the attack on Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did the reservists ever tell you anything about Zec's role in the events of the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Not to me personally. You're reading from the statement, and that is all the things I heard from them, from their conversations. It's not that the reservists ever came up to me and said, "Hey, such-and-such a person gave an order," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So if nobody ever addressed you -- so this conversation that you overheard, did it take place on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't know what's written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I've already read out to you what is written there and now I'm trying to obtain information from you, from whom you heard this and when. So since no one told you that, you say that you overheard the conversation of other people, then I'm asking you when it was that you overheard this conversation of these other people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the Prosecution, you say: "I think that I saw him once or twice during the entire action." Am I right when I say that when you saw Zec on television two years ago, you came to the conclusion that you perhaps saw him once or twice on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I think that perhaps that was misinterpreted. Throughout those four months, I saw him perhaps once or twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where was the sun when Captain Kovacevic lined you up and said that Dubrovnik had to be surrendered within half an hour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I didn't look at the sky then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was it after daybreak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, a bit, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where is the sun during the winter around 7.00?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was the first objective of that attack that you're talking about of the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: You mean the first objective that was targeted?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The first objective in general.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The first objective that was targeted was Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were there any provocations from the Croatian side at the time when you came to Zarkovica and all the way up to the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any provocations after the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there ever any provocations from the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you be a little more careful with your microphone and your pauses, Mr. Petrovic. There are problems --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm really making an effort, but I realise that the effort is inadequate, and I'll try to do better.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why, then, did you tell the investigator of this Tribunal on the 15th of June -- or, rather, 2002, why did you say there were provocations from both sides involving infantry weapons but there weren't any casualties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Not at Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where is -- excuse me, where is counsel referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to read the whole paragraph now and then it would be clear to you precisely because of this answer. This is how it starts -- it's page 6 in B/C/S, towards the bottom of the page. Unfortunately, at this moment I cannot tell you where it is in English, but I'll try. Page 6 in English, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: "Between the 6th of November and the 6th of December [as interpreted], there were routine activities going on at Zarkovica. We maintained combat readiness. More weapons were brought in, mostly Maljutkas, and rocket were dug in. There were provocations with infantry weapons from both sides." You clearly refer to Zarkovica there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes. Bullets could be heard, but not a single bullet passed via Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What kind of Croatian provocations were there when you say they came from both sides?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were provocations. When an automatic rifle is heard somewhere, when someone is shooting from the automatic rifle. I don't know. But not a single bullet reached Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There's a problem with the record. Page 83, line 20. It says: "Between the 6th of November and the 6th of December." The language in the report says: "Between the 19th of November."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying it should be between the 19th of November and the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's verbatim from the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It was wrongly quoted in the transcript. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I read the 19th in the Serbian language. There must have been some mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So what kind of provocations coming from both sides are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: In my opinion, a provocation is if somebody uses an automatic rifle to shoot at a position. However, there were no bullets fired at our positions. Even if a burst of gunfire was heard somewhere in the area around Dubrovnik, there was a sniper shooter who was in charge of doing that, targeting a boat on sea or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So, from Dubrovnik until the 6th of December, nobody fired a single bullet; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I think no one did. At least I'm not aware of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, then -- I'm going to find this part of your statement now. Why do you say that you were under the constant threat of sniper fire? Can you give me an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, where is he referring to? Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I perhaps have a look at that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's still being identified. If you would just be a little patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be of assistance now, of course, to the witness and to my learned friend and, first and foremost, of course, to the Honourable Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to my colleague Mr. Weiner during these past several days before testifying here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. Weiner about this, what the truth was to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, here in Mr. Weiner's record, and he is certainly very conscientious in attending to his duties, on page 3, paragraph 1, it says: [Previous translation continues] ... "[In English] ... could be hit by sniper fire. There was no sniper fire, however, into Zarkovica on that day." [Interpretation] That's what you said to Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Weiner, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's right. And being conscientious, it says the witness was still cautious that they could be hit by sniper fire, but there was no sniper fire that day. There's no statement in there that was indicating that there was a great deal of sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, throughout this time I've been talking about the period from the 19th of November until the 6th of December. I'm not talking about the 6th of December. I emphasise that. And you even corrected me, Mr. Weiner, or rather, you corrected the transcript. So I'm asking the witness about his statement about the period from the 19th of November until the 6th of December. I thought that that was clear at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying that in that statement in respect of the period from the 19th of November to the 6th of December he says there was sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the statement he gave to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 15th of June, 2002, he says: "Between the 19th of November and the 6th of December, there were provocations with infantry weapons." And he says to Mr. Weiner that he was very careful because he was afraid of sniper fire. On that day there was no sniper fire. If there was no sniper fire on that day and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When do you say he said that to Mr. Weiner? Are you speaking of his evidence in this Chamber or an earlier statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm referring to the proofing session that Mr. Weiner had with Witness B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. That hadn't become clear to me. Well, we're having a considerable debate over the true effect of these various statements, and a lot of the reason for that is that you are not following the conventional way of putting to a witness that he has been inconsistent, which would be to say, "Your evidence is X. Did you not say something different on a previous occasion?" The witness will say yes or no. If the witness says no, for you to show the witness where something different was said the previous occasion and ask for the witness's comment. You're not doing that for reasons which you have indicated, and that's leading us now to this great debate as to what was said and where and what really was its effect when the language is generally not crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for what you've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to Mr. Weiner about sniper fire at Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you mention sniper fire to him at all in the entire interview you had with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I can't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did you talk to Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: About two weeks ago and yesterday and today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Today? When today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: In the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And in none of these situations you mentioned snipers to Mr. Weiner. You never mentioned it to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I can't remember. I told him about what he asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, for how long did Captain Kovacevic speak to you that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Approximately five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did he tell you exactly that morning? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: That the surrender of Dubrovnik is expected, and if Dubrovnik does not surrender by such-and-such a time that it would be attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What else did he tell you? Five minutes is a long time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I can't remember the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who was it that he said this to? Who were all the people present there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The soldiers, we who were at Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many soldiers were there, Mr. B?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: About 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did they all hear this, what he said to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No. Those who were on guard duty could not hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All of those people who were lined up, did they hear the same words that you are testifying about here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't know if everybody heard all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the hour and in view of how far I got in the cross-examination, and I believe that I have assured you that I am putting questions only in respect of our case here, I kindly ask you to allow me to continue putting questions tomorrow as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is the view of the Tribunal, which we have given some consideration to, that you will be allowed to continue tomorrow, but we would think you should plan to conclude in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And we've now reached the time to close the session. We will now adjourn. After we've left, preparations will be made for the witness to leave the Chamber and we will resume tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 21st day of April, 2004, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
